topics.label: Sustainability as a professional duty
topics.must_understand: GMP 2024 Domain 1 includes 'Managing resources effectively and sustainably' — NEW in 2024. That healthcare has a material carbon footprint and that sustainable practice is now framed as a duty rather than an interest.
topics.assessment: Policy discussion or follow-up.
weak: Treating sustainability as unrelated to clinical practice
danger: Absent from any content mapped to the 2013 GMP domains

topics.label: Ethics of international recruitment
topics.must_understand: The tension between the NHS's historic dependence on international medical graduates, the 10 Year Health Plan target of under 10% international recruitment by 2035, the prioritisation legislation, and the effect on source countries' health systems.
topics.assessment: Policy discussion with hostile follow-up.
weak: One-sided argument in either direction
danger: Handle with care. A candidate may be an IMG's child or an international applicant. Never signal a position; probe both directions equally.

topics.label: Applying school science to a novel problem
topics.must_understand: Cambridge's published expectation: sixth-form Chemistry, Biology, Maths and Physics applied to novel scenarios, with lateral thinking and conceptual flexibility, observation and hypothesis generation.
topics.assessment: Scientific problem with the interviewer prompting rather than correcting.
weak: Recalling a memorised answer
Silence rather than thinking aloud
Guessing without stating the reasoning
danger: SCORING RULE: score the reasoning path, explicitly not the answer. An incorrect conclusion reached by good reasoning outscores a correct one asserted.

topics.label: Hypothesis generation from an observation
topics.must_understand: Generating several candidate explanations, then proposing what would distinguish them.
topics.assessment: Scientific problem.
weak: One hypothesis, asserted
No test proposed
danger: Oxbridge routes only — 4 of 68. Do not spend Phase 1 budget here.

topics.label: Thinking aloud under an interviewer's prompts
topics.must_understand: That the tutorial format expects an audible reasoning process and responsiveness to hints; Oxford lists 'compatibility with tutorial format' as a criterion.
topics.assessment: Scientific problem with graded hints.
weak: Long silences
Ignoring a hint
Abandoning a line of reasoning at the first difficulty
danger: Our interviewer must hint the way a tutor does — narrowing the space, not supplying the answer. See Output 7 on leading.

topics.label: Correlation and causation
topics.must_understand: That an association does not establish causation, and what would be needed — temporality, dose-response, plausibility, controlling for confounders, ideally randomisation.
topics.assessment: Article discussion or data interpretation.
weak: Naming the distinction without identifying the confounder in front of them
danger: ANTI-BUZZWORD: 'correlation does not imply causation' scores nothing on its own. Naming a specific plausible confounder scores.

topics.label: Sample, bias and generalisability
topics.must_understand: Who was studied, who was left out, and whether the result transfers to the population in question.
topics.assessment: Article discussion.
weak: Accepting a headline claim at face value
danger: Do not require study-design vocabulary. Reward the question, not the term.

topics.label: Absolute versus relative risk
topics.must_understand: That a 50% increase in a small risk is still a small risk, and that media reporting systematically prefers relative figures.
topics.assessment: Data interpretation with a deliberately misleading headline.
weak: Reacting to the relative figure without asking for the baseline
danger: The highest-yield single critical-appraisal skill for a 17-year-old, and it needs no medical knowledge.

topics.label: Reading a claim in the media
topics.must_understand: Who made the claim, who funded it, what was actually measured, and what the headline omits.
topics.assessment: Article discussion — also the Keele pre-read format.
weak: Discussing the topic rather than appraising the source
danger: Keele issues a case study 1-2 days before interview and tells candidates they are not expected to memorise it. Our pre-read mode should mirror that instruction.

topics.label: Percentages, ratios and proportions under time pressure
topics.must_understand: Fluent mental arithmetic at or below GCSE level, with the method spoken aloud.
topics.assessment: Calculation station, no calculator. Leicester runs this with a pass-mark threshold; Birmingham runs it computer-based with clinically relevant but GCSE-level data.
weak: Silent calculation with only an answer
Not sanity-checking an implausible result
danger: Score method transparency as well as accuracy — a spoken method allows partial credit and mirrors how these stations are marked.

topics.label: Units, conversion and estimation
topics.must_understand: Converting between units without error, and producing a defensible order-of-magnitude estimate.
topics.assessment: Calculation station.
weak: Unit errors going unnoticed
danger: Keep all framing non-clinical or clinically trivial. Never require drug-dosing knowledge.

topics.label: Reading a chart or table accurately
topics.must_understand: Axes, units, scale, time period, and what is actually plotted.
topics.assessment: Data interpretation station.
weak: Describing the shape without reading the axes
Extrapolating beyond the data
danger: QUB states explicitly there are no data or graph stations; Manchester has no reading at all. Serve data stations only where the school profile supports them.

topics.label: Stating what the data cannot show
topics.must_understand: That the highest-value response names the limits — no comparator, no denominator, truncated axis, aggregation hiding variation.
topics.assessment: Data interpretation with MISLEAD set high.
weak: Answering only what was asked
Accepting the presentation uncritically
danger: This is the discriminating behaviour and should be weighted above arithmetic accuracy.

topics.label: AI in healthcare — what it does
topics.must_understand: That AI in the NHS is currently strongest in triage, documentation and image analysis rather than autonomous diagnosis. As at 2026: NHS England announced an AI acceleration on 4 July 2026 within a £10bn three-year technology programme — AI triage in the NHS App, ambient voice documentation in outpatients, Copilot for 500,000+ staff.
topics.assessment: Policy discussion.
weak: 'AI will replace doctors' or 'AI will never replace doctors' with no mechanism
Discussing AI in general rather than in a named use case
danger: FAST. The tester named this as a gap. Review quarterly.

topics.label: AI accountability and regulation
topics.must_understand: That the GMC's position is that accountability does NOT transfer — practitioners remain responsible for decisions taken using new technologies, must discuss their use with patients including uncertainties and limitations, must work within their competence, and must report adverse incidents involving software and digital tools. On 29 July 2026 the MHRA clarified that transcription, summarisation and letter drafting are not medical devices, while ambient voice technology that supports diagnosis or acts without clinician review IS a regulated medical device.
topics.assessment: Policy discussion with hostile follow-up: 'If the AI was wrong, who is responsible?'
weak: Not addressing accountability at all
Assuming the manufacturer bears clinical responsibility
danger: This is the single best-differentiated AI sub-question and almost nobody teaches it. The regulatory boundary is unstable — a functionality change can silently alter a product's regulatory status.

topics.label: AI bias, deskilling and trust
topics.must_understand: That training-data bias can widen inequity, that automation bias makes clinicians over-trust outputs, and that deskilling is a live concern as documentation and triage become default.
topics.assessment: Policy discussion.
weak: Naming 'bias' with no mechanism or example
danger: A candidate who can name a mechanism — under-representation in training data leading to worse performance in a subgroup — substantially outperforms one who names the word.

topics.label: Health data, consent and public trust
topics.must_understand: The tension between data-driven care and consent at scale; the Single Patient Record confirmed in the King's Speech on 13 May 2026 within the NHS Modernisation Bill; the Federated Data Platform controversy, including reporting in May 2026 that NHS England planned to grant Palantir and external consultancy staff admin-level access to identifiable patient data, with an internal briefing acknowledging risk of loss of public confidence.
topics.assessment: Policy discussion.
weak: Treating data sharing as either obviously good or obviously sinister
danger: FAST and contested. Present both the care-improvement case and the trust case; never signal a position.

topics.label: Digital exclusion
topics.must_understand: That making the NHS App the front door disadvantages people without smartphones, connectivity, digital skills or English — disproportionately older, poorer and disabled people, who use care most. This is the inverse care law restated for the digital era.
topics.assessment: Policy discussion.
weak: Discussing digital transformation with no equity dimension
danger: A high-value link between two topics most candidates treat separately. Reward the connection.

topics.label: Genomics and its consequences
topics.must_understand: That genomic medicine is moving from diagnosis of rare disease toward population stratification — newborn genomic screening, targeted screening by genetic risk — and that this creates consent, incidental-finding, insurance and equity problems.
topics.assessment: Policy discussion.
weak: Enthusiasm with no downside
Confusing genomic screening with genetic engineering
danger: Newborn genomic screening raises consent for someone who cannot consent, and a finding that cannot be un-known. That tension is the assessable content.
